horizon_driver: multi-year collective-bargaining contract cycle (e.g., ILA's six-year master contract) punctuated by acute leverage windows at contract expiry

constraints.action: wildcat strike without union executive authorization
constraints.source: US labor law (no-strike clauses in active contracts) and union governance norms
constraints.breaks_under: membership anger outruns leadership caution — has occurred in isolated European rail actions where strikes were called with reduced notice

stated_vs_revealed.stated: The ILA's public position in 2024 emphasized wages as the headline contract issue.
stated_vs_revealed.revealed: The October 2024 strike (45,000 dockworkers, 36 East/Gulf Coast ports, ~$5bn/day in stranded trade) was resolved on wages within 3 days (61.5% increase over 6 years, $39 to ~$63/hr), but the harder-fought issue — a full ban on port automation — remained unresolved and pushed final contract ratification out to January 2025.
stated_vs_revealed.delta: The headline (wage) issue resolved fast; the real binding constraint (automation/job security) is what actually determined the negotiation timeline, confirming the Cartographer's framing that a few thousand port workers can halt more trade than most sanctions regimes.

stated_vs_revealed.stated: European rail unions (e.g., Germany's GDL) frame recurring strikes as discrete, pay-dispute-driven events.
stated_vs_revealed.revealed: GDL executed its announced 35-hour strike in March 2024 and signaled willingness to strike again without the usual 48-hour notice; combined German/Dutch/Belgian labor disputes and rail-corridor closures produced the most sustained European port/freight congestion crisis since the pandemic through 2025.
stated_vs_revealed.delta: Individually-framed 'discrete' pay disputes are revealed, in aggregate, as a structural and repeated freight-chokepoint tool rather than isolated events.

tripwires.if: a major port/rail contract nears expiry without a pre-agreed automation or job-security protection clause
tripwires.then: strike probability spikes sharply in the final weeks before expiry, with costs on the order of ~$5bn/day for a major US port action (2024 ILA precedent)

tripwires.if: strike-notice requirements are shortened or bypassed (as GDL signaled)
tripwires.then: logistics planners lose lead time to reroute, and disruption severity per strike-day rises even if strike frequency stays flat

what_would_change_my_mind: A major contract expiry (e.g., a successor to ILA's Jan 2025 deal, or a comparable European rail agreement) resolving without any strike action or credible strike threat despite unresolved automation/staffing issues would suggest strike leverage in logistics has weakened structurally. This dossier covers only US and European (DM) logistics labor; Asian and Global South port/rail action, which faces thinner union density and more state suppression, was not researched here and should not be generalized from this pass.
